bull_bear.body:
- Scale and irreplicability of the asset platform - the AR states IRB commands a group asset base of approximately Rs 94,000 Cr and describes a portfolio 'that stands without a true peer in the Indian roads sector'
- Dual InvIT structure (a sponsored Public InvIT and a Private InvIT) that the report calls 'a setup that few domestic peers can replicate', giving capital-recycling optionality
- Largest private TOT operator - the AR cites a 43% share of the awarded TOT space, 'the largest by any private player in the sector'
- Network share of national tolling - IRB and its Private InvIT contributed over 10% of India's national toll revenue in FY 2025-26
- In-house integrated construction and O&M capability, so concessions are executed and maintained without third-party EPC dependence
- B.E.S.T. operating discipline (Bid, Execute, Stabilise, Transfer) that recycles equity multiple times rather than locking it into an asset for decades
- Institutional partner base - GIC (Singapore sovereign wealth fund) and Cintra N.E., a fully-owned subsidiary of Ferrovial Group of Spain
- Long-dated concession contracts with government counterparties producing recurring toll and annuity cash flows
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Concession expiry or termination at project SPV level — The Board's Report names 'Expiry or termination of the project Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) respective concession Agreements' among the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations. Because every toll asset sits inside a finite-life concession, the revenue base is contractually time-bound and terminable, making this the most structural risk in the business model.
- Regulatory change and government policy in the transportation sector — Cited twice in the forward-looking statement: 'regulatory changes pertaining to the infrastructure sector in India and the Company's ability to respond to them' and 'Regulatory changes and future government policy relating to the transportation industry in India'. Tariff-setting, concession terms and award models (BOT/TOT/HAM) are all set by NHAI and the Ministry, so policy shifts move economics directly.
- Traffic growth and transportation industry environment — The Board's Report flags 'The general transportation industry environment and traffic growth' as a factor that could cause results to differ materially. Toll revenue is a direct function of vehicle volumes, so an economic or freight slowdown flows straight through to collections.
- Execution of strategy, growth and expansion plans — The forward-looking statement identifies 'the Company's ability to successfully implement its strategy and objectives' and 'the Company's growth and expansion plans' as risk factors, alongside 'The business and investment strategy of the Company'. With growth now dependent on asset rotation and redeployment rather than build-out, execution slippage in that cycle is a structural exposure.
- Financing, liquidity and future cash flow — The Board's Report lists 'Future earnings, cash flow and liquidity' and 'Financing plans' among the factors that could cause material variance. Highway concessions are capital-intensive and debt-funded, so financing availability and refinancing terms are a persistent structural dependency.
- Interest rate, foreign exchange and market-rate exposure — The forward-looking statement names 'unanticipated turbulence in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity prices or other rates or prices' and 'the Company's exposure to market risks', adding that 'certain market risk disclosures are only estimates and could be materially different from what actually occurs in the future'.
- Competition in the infrastructure sector — The Board's Report flags 'changes in competition in the infrastructure sector' and 'The competitive position and the effects of competition on the Company's investments'. Concessions are awarded through competitive bidding, so bid discipline versus aggressive rivals determines returns on new assets.
- Macroeconomic conditions, inflation and fiscal/monetary policy in India — The forward-looking statement cites 'general economic and political conditions in India that have an impact on the Company's business activities or investments, the monetary and fiscal policies of India, inflation, deflation' and 'the performance of the financial markets in India and globally', plus 'changes in domestic laws, regulations and taxes'. As a purely India-facing infrastructure operator, IRB carries undiversified country exposure.

business.body: IRB builds, owns, operates and monetises toll-road and highway infrastructure in India under BOT, TOT and HAM concession models, with in-house construction and O&M capability and no third-party EPC work undertaken. Its portfolio includes landmark assets such as the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, Ahmedabad-Vadodara Expressway and the Hyderabad Outer Ring Road, plus one airport project. Concessions are held through three listed vehicles - IRB Infra itself and two InvIT platforms (a sponsored Public InvIT, IRB InvIT Fund, and a Private InvIT, IRB Infrastructure Trust) - into which mature assets are rotated to recycle capital.

outlook.body:
- B.E.S.T. philosophy - Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer: a continuous, disciplined rotation of assets so that every rupee of equity is made to work multiple times over rather than being committed once and held for decades
- Value rotation through InvIT platforms - transferring stabilised assets into the sponsored Public and Private InvITs to unlock capital, strengthen financial flexibility and create capacity for future investments
- Completing the shift from contractor to developer to institutional owner-operator, running as a Sponsor and O&M-led platform focused on capital efficiency, recurring cash flows and long-term annuity income
- Disciplined capital allocation with a stated objective of reaching a net debt-free consolidated position over the next five years to improve financial resilience and cash return on equity
- Redeploying recycled capital into new highway concessions to keep growing the underlying portfolio, including expanding geographic footprint (Odisha added via TOT-18)
- Technology adoption treated as an enabler of safer roads, better customer service and more efficient operations rather than an end in itself
- Embedding ESG considerations - climate and energy, resource circularity, water stewardship, biodiversity, safe and inclusive workplaces - into asset design, project selection and execution rather than as standalone initiatives
- Enterprise risk management aligned to COSO ERM 2017 with a Board-constituted Risk Management Committee setting a formal risk appetite statement
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: IRB describes FY 2025-26 as the year its build-out phase closed: 'All major projects are now operational. The capex cycle is complete.' The group asset base rose to approximately Rs 94,000 Cr from around Rs 80,000 Cr at the start of the year, spanning 28 highway assets across 13 states plus one airport project. Expansion during the year came through concession additions and asset rotation rather than greenfield capex on the parent balance sheet. Ganga Expressway Group 1, covering the Meerut-to-Budaun corridor of 129.7 km, was inaugurated by the Prime Minister. IRB bagged the Chandikhole-Bhadrak NH16 TOT-18 Bundle from NHAI and commenced tolling, extending its footprint into Odisha. Under the B.E.S.T. rotation, mature operational assets worth Rs 8,436 Cr were transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund (Public InvIT), unlocking equity capital of nearly Rs 4,905 Cr, while the Private InvIT redeployed capital into expanding the portfolio by approximately Rs 14,000 Cr in enterprise value. The Gandeva-Ena VM7 Hybrid Annuity asset, part of the Delhi-Mumbai Greenfield Expressway, was transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund, bringing in around Rs 510 Cr towards equity investment while consolidated debt reduced by approximately Rs 700 Cr. In the prior year IRB had received the TOT-17 bundle (Lucknow-Ayodhya-Gorakhpur NH27 and Lucknow-Sultanpur NH731) with a cost outlay of Rs 10,490 Cr and commenced tolling. Going forward the company states growth will come from operating leverage, rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation and recurring O&M income, alongside a stated objective of reaching a net debt-free consolidated position over the next five years.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India remains one of the world's fastest-growing major economies; despite geopolitical uncertainty and global volatility, economic resilience continued to drive growth in both passenger mobility and freight movement
- Healthy traffic growth across the portfolio and stronger toll collections, particularly in the second half of the year
- Toll revenue across IRB and its Private InvIT platform grew by nearly 13% year-on-year, driven by healthy traffic growth, periodic tariff revisions and the addition of new operational assets
- With the capex cycle complete and all major projects operational, future growth is expected from operating leverage, rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation and recurring O&M income
- Highways serve nearly 1.5 Mn vehicles every day and account for close to 10% of India's total toll collections, giving a broad base for tariff-linked revenue
- Group asset base rose to approximately Rs 94,000 Cr from around Rs 80,000 Cr at the start of the year, reflecting portfolio expansion
- Recurring O&M income and long-term annuity flows are expected to sharpen earnings visibility as the business mix shifts to an owner-operator model
- IRB Group operates 28 highway assets across 13 states, with the network generating over Rs 1 Cr in toll revenue every hour
- The Private InvIT redeployed capital into expanding the portfolio by approximately Rs 14,000 Cr in enterprise value during FY 2025-26
- Mature operational assets worth Rs 8,436 Cr were transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund (Public InvIT) during the year, unlocking equity capital of nearly Rs 4,905 Cr

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India remains one of the world's fastest-growing major economies; despite geopolitical uncertainty and global volatility, economic resilience continued to drive growth in both passenger mobility and freight movement
- Healthy traffic growth across the portfolio and stronger toll collections, particularly in the second half of the year
- Toll revenue across IRB and its Private InvIT platform grew by nearly 13% year-on-year, driven by healthy traffic growth, periodic tariff revisions and the addition of new operational assets
- With the capex cycle complete and all major projects operational, future growth is expected from operating leverage, rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation and recurring O&M income
- Highways serve nearly 1.5 Mn vehicles every day and account for close to 10% of India's total toll collections, giving a broad base for tariff-linked revenue
- Group asset base rose to approximately Rs 94,000 Cr from around Rs 80,000 Cr at the start of the year, reflecting portfolio expansion
- Recurring O&M income and long-term annuity flows are expected to sharpen earnings visibility as the business mix shifts to an owner-operator model
- IRB Group operates 28 highway assets across 13 states, with the network generating over Rs 1 Cr in toll revenue every hour
- The Private InvIT redeployed capital into expanding the portfolio by approximately Rs 14,000 Cr in enterprise value during FY 2025-26
- Mature operational assets worth Rs 8,436 Cr were transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund (Public InvIT) during the year, unlocking equity capital of nearly Rs 4,905 Cr

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- B.E.S.T. philosophy - Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer: a continuous, disciplined rotation of assets so that every rupee of equity is made to work multiple times over rather than being committed once and held for decades
- Value rotation through InvIT platforms - transferring stabilised assets into the sponsored Public and Private InvITs to unlock capital, strengthen financial flexibility and create capacity for future investments
- Completing the shift from contractor to developer to institutional owner-operator, running as a Sponsor and O&M-led platform focused on capital efficiency, recurring cash flows and long-term annuity income
- Disciplined capital allocation with a stated objective of reaching a net debt-free consolidated position over the next five years to improve financial resilience and cash return on equity
- Redeploying recycled capital into new highway concessions to keep growing the underlying portfolio, including expanding geographic footprint (Odisha added via TOT-18)
- Technology adoption treated as an enabler of safer roads, better customer service and more efficient operations rather than an end in itself
- Embedding ESG considerations - climate and energy, resource circularity, water stewardship, biodiversity, safe and inclusive workplaces - into asset design, project selection and execution rather than as standalone initiatives
- Enterprise risk management aligned to COSO ERM 2017 with a Board-constituted Risk Management Committee setting a formal risk appetite statement

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: IRB describes FY 2025-26 as the year its build-out phase closed: 'All major projects are now operational. The capex cycle is complete.' The group asset base rose to approximately Rs 94,000 Cr from around Rs 80,000 Cr at the start of the year, spanning 28 highway assets across 13 states plus one airport project. Expansion during the year came through concession additions and asset rotation rather than greenfield capex on the parent balance sheet. Ganga Expressway Group 1, covering the Meerut-to-Budaun corridor of 129.7 km, was inaugurated by the Prime Minister. IRB bagged the Chandikhole-Bhadrak NH16 TOT-18 Bundle from NHAI and commenced tolling, extending its footprint into Odisha. Under the B.E.S.T. rotation, mature operational assets worth Rs 8,436 Cr were transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund (Public InvIT), unlocking equity capital of nearly Rs 4,905 Cr, while the Private InvIT redeployed capital into expanding the portfolio by approximately Rs 14,000 Cr in enterprise value. The Gandeva-Ena VM7 Hybrid Annuity asset, part of the Delhi-Mumbai Greenfield Expressway, was transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund, bringing in around Rs 510 Cr towards equity investment while consolidated debt reduced by approximately Rs 700 Cr. In the prior year IRB had received the TOT-17 bundle (Lucknow-Ayodhya-Gorakhpur NH27 and Lucknow-Sultanpur NH731) with a cost outlay of Rs 10,490 Cr and commenced tolling. Going forward the company states growth will come from operating leverage, rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation and recurring O&M income, alongside a stated objective of reaching a net debt-free consolidated position over the next five years.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Scale and irreplicability of the asset platform - the AR states IRB commands a group asset base of approximately Rs 94,000 Cr and describes a portfolio 'that stands without a true peer in the Indian roads sector'
- Dual InvIT structure (a sponsored Public InvIT and a Private InvIT) that the report calls 'a setup that few domestic peers can replicate', giving capital-recycling optionality
- Largest private TOT operator - the AR cites a 43% share of the awarded TOT space, 'the largest by any private player in the sector'
- Network share of national tolling - IRB and its Private InvIT contributed over 10% of India's national toll revenue in FY 2025-26
- In-house integrated construction and O&M capability, so concessions are executed and maintained without third-party EPC dependence
- B.E.S.T. operating discipline (Bid, Execute, Stabilise, Transfer) that recycles equity multiple times rather than locking it into an asset for decades
- Institutional partner base - GIC (Singapore sovereign wealth fund) and Cintra N.E., a fully-owned subsidiary of Ferrovial Group of Spain
- Long-dated concession contracts with government counterparties producing recurring toll and annuity cash flows

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Concession expiry or termination at project SPV level — The Board's Report names 'Expiry or termination of the project Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) respective concession Agreements' among the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations. Because every toll asset sits inside a finite-life concession, the revenue base is contractually time-bound and terminable, making this the most structural risk in the business model.
- Regulatory change and government policy in the transportation sector — Cited twice in the forward-looking statement: 'regulatory changes pertaining to the infrastructure sector in India and the Company's ability to respond to them' and 'Regulatory changes and future government policy relating to the transportation industry in India'. Tariff-setting, concession terms and award models (BOT/TOT/HAM) are all set by NHAI and the Ministry, so policy shifts move economics directly.
- Traffic growth and transportation industry environment — The Board's Report flags 'The general transportation industry environment and traffic growth' as a factor that could cause results to differ materially. Toll revenue is a direct function of vehicle volumes, so an economic or freight slowdown flows straight through to collections.
- Execution of strategy, growth and expansion plans — The forward-looking statement identifies 'the Company's ability to successfully implement its strategy and objectives' and 'the Company's growth and expansion plans' as risk factors, alongside 'The business and investment strategy of the Company'. With growth now dependent on asset rotation and redeployment rather than build-out, execution slippage in that cycle is a structural exposure.
- Financing, liquidity and future cash flow — The Board's Report lists 'Future earnings, cash flow and liquidity' and 'Financing plans' among the factors that could cause material variance. Highway concessions are capital-intensive and debt-funded, so financing availability and refinancing terms are a persistent structural dependency.
- Interest rate, foreign exchange and market-rate exposure — The forward-looking statement names 'unanticipated turbulence in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity prices or other rates or prices' and 'the Company's exposure to market risks', adding that 'certain market risk disclosures are only estimates and could be materially different from what actually occurs in the future'.
- Competition in the infrastructure sector — The Board's Report flags 'changes in competition in the infrastructure sector' and 'The competitive position and the effects of competition on the Company's investments'. Concessions are awarded through competitive bidding, so bid discipline versus aggressive rivals determines returns on new assets.
- Macroeconomic conditions, inflation and fiscal/monetary policy in India — The forward-looking statement cites 'general economic and political conditions in India that have an impact on the Company's business activities or investments, the monetary and fiscal policies of India, inflation, deflation' and 'the performance of the financial markets in India and globally', plus 'changes in domestic laws, regulations and taxes'. As a purely India-facing infrastructure operator, IRB carries undiversified country exposure.

themes.title: Infrastructure EPC & roads order-book conversion
themes.need: India's record capital-outlay cycle (roads, metro, marine, hydro, tunnelling) gives diversified EPC contractors multi-year visibility - AFCONS tracks a ~INR4 lakh cr pipeline (70% domestic) and targets ~INR30,000cr FY27 inflow; NCC/DBL/PNCINFRA/GRINFRA/ASHOKA/CEIGALL carry large road/HAM books; AFCONS/PATELENG/AHLUCONT/PSPPROJECT add marine, hydro and building EPC. The binding issue is execution + client-payment cycles, not order intake.
